getting_started.title: Getting started
getting_started.content:
Slate

Slate is the studio's pipeline and its people system in one application. This help follows whatever screen you are on — press F1 at any time and you land on the page for it.

What you see is decided by what you are

Slate does not have a mode switch, and it does not show you screens you cannot act on. The same sidebar entry opens a different screen depending on your role:

EntryIf you are an artistIf you are HR or IT
LeaveYour balance, and a button to ask for time off The approval queue
IT SupportYour tickets and their replies The service desk
Joining & LeavingNot shown at all Your team's half of the checklist

So if a colleague describes a button you cannot find, you are probably both right — you are looking at different screens.

Getting around

KeyDoes
F1Help for the screen you are on
F11Full screen
EscClose this window

The sidebar collapses to icons with the arrow at its foot, which is worth doing on a laptop. Sections (PRODUCTION, HRMS, IT & INFRA) fold away if you never use them.

If something looks wrong

A figure looks stale. Press Sync in the header. The number beside it is the round trip to the studio database in milliseconds.

Slate says it is in fallback mode. It could not reach the studio database and has started on a local copy instead. You can keep working, but nothing you do is shared until the connection is back. Tell IT.

Something is genuinely broken. Raise it in IT Support rather than messaging somebody — a ticket carries a clock and a message does not.

home.title: Home
home.content:
Home

The opening screen. Three things on it.

Quick launch

The four screens most people open first. Shortcuts, nothing more.

My recent tasks

Shots assigned to you. Empty means nothing is assigned — not that something failed.

Live studio telemetry

The studio in five numbers: active projects, shots pending review, artists online, open IT tickets and upcoming leave. They are read from the studio database, so they are the same numbers your supervisor sees.

If every figure reads zero and you expected otherwise, check the header for fallback mode — a local database has no studio in it.

attendance.title: Attendance
attendance.content:
Attendance

Punch in when you start, out when you finish. That is the whole screen.

Why it matters beyond the record

If your studio operates comp-off, this is what earns it. Slate reads the punch data and credits the ledger — it is never typed in by hand, and never credited twice for the same day.

Three ways a day qualifies, and a studio may operate any combination:

  • You worked a weekly off (Sunday)
  • You worked a public holiday
  • You worked a long enough shift

A shift that crosses midnight is counted properly rather than thrown away as bad data — in a crunch week that is usually the shift that earned the comp-off in the first place.

If you forgot to punch

You cannot edit the record yourself, on purpose. Ask HR — a correction that anyone can make is not a record.

Where it shows up

Your comp-off balance appears on the Leave screen. If your studio does not operate comp-off it reads zero and says so, which is correct rather than broken.

leave.title: Leave
leave.content:
Leave

Two entirely different screens sit behind this entry. Which one you get depends on whether you approve other people's leave.

If you are asking for leave

Four figures across the top:

FigureMeans
AvailableWhat you can actually take right now
AccruedEarned since you joined — two days for every completed month
Awaiting approvalDays held by requests nobody has decided yet
Comp offEarned by working a weekly off or a long day, where the studio operates it

Available already has your pending requests subtracted. Ask for five days and then five more before the first is decided, and the second is measured against what would be left.

Why a day off sometimes costs three

Press Request leave and the dialog shows the cost before you commit.

The studio works Monday to Saturday; Sunday is the weekly off. Public holidays are free. But a working day that sits between two non-working days, where you do not come in, charges the whole block — the sandwich rule.

Monday is a holiday.  Tuesday is a working day.  Wednesday is a holiday.
Take Tuesday off  ->  you are charged three days, not one.

The dialog spells this out as you pick the dates. If the number surprises you, the reason is written underneath it. A half day costs 0.5.

What happens next

Your request goes to your supervisor first, then to HR. It is only deducted once both have said yes. The Waiting on column tells you whose desk it is on.

If it is rejected you get the reason — Slate does not let anyone reject a request without writing one.

If you approve leave

The screen opens on Waiting on me. Sorting is deliberate: yours first, then soonest starting, because somebody leaving on Monday needs an answer before somebody leaving next month.

You can only act on requests at your own stage. Selecting one that is still with the other approver leaves the buttons off rather than failing when you press them.

Approve tells you where it goes next before you confirm, because approval means different things at the two stages. Reject asks for a reason, and the person who asked will read it.

HR only

Calendar — the studio's public holidays. Every date on it is free, and the sandwich rule is measured against it, so it is worth doing in one sitting at the start of the year. Removing a holiday does not rewrite history: leave already taken keeps the day count it was charged at.

Year end — closes a leave year. Up to the carry-forward cap moves into the next year and the rest lapses. It previews exactly who loses what before anything is written, will not close the same year twice, and defaults to the year just gone rather than the one you are still in.

it_support.title: IT Support
it_support.content:
IT Support

Your tickets, or the whole queue, depending on whether you work in IT.

Raising one

Two questions decide how fast it gets picked up. Answer them honestly rather than strategically — you do not choose the priority, and that is what keeps the queue trustworthy.

Who is affected?

  • The whole studio, or a service everyone depends on
  • My department, or several people
  • Only me

Can you carry on?

  • I cannot work at all — there is no way around it
  • I have a workaround, but it is costing me real time
  • I can carry on. This can wait.

Slate works the priority out from those two answers:

Cannot workWorkaroundCan wait
Whole studioP1P2P2
A departmentP2P3P3
One personP3P3P4

Afterwards

The ticket shows who picked it up, or Not yet picked up if nobody has. Open it to read the conversation and reply.

When IT need something from you it moves to Waiting on you. Watch for that one — the clock is paused on their side and running on yours.

If you work the queue

It opens sorted the way you should work it: breached first, then at risk, then by priority, then by how long is left.

PriorityRespond withinResolve within
P115 minutes4 hours
P230 minutes8 hours
P32 hours3 days
P44 hours5 days

Take assigns it to you. Mark responded stops the response clock — press it when you actually reply, not when you open the ticket. Response is attention; resolution is a fix.

settings.title: Settings
settings.content:
Settings

Per-machine preferences. Nothing here changes anything for anybody else.

Where the studio is

The database host, port and name. These are written once by setup.bat and stored outside the application folder, so an update does not lose them.

If Slate starts in fallback mode, this is the first place to look — but it is usually the server or the network rather than these values.

Paths

Where projects, scans and the stock library live. Slate maps drive letters across Windows, Mac and Linux, so a path written on one platform resolves on another.

Performance

Thumbnail cache size and how many background jobs run at once. Turn them down on a modest workstation; the defaults suit a comp machine.

Your password

Changed here. It is stored as a one-way hash — nobody, including an administrator, can read it back.

folder_creator.title: Build & Ingest
folder_creator.content:
Build & Ingest

Turn a client drive into a project, and keep it fed afterwards.

Building a new project

  1. Enter the project code — PRJ_001, AK74, whatever the studio uses.
  2. Point Source at the client or incoming drive.
  3. Leave Reel empty to let Slate work it out from the folder names, or name one.
  4. Pick the template. That decides the folder structure every shot gets.
  5. Build & Move Files.

Slate reads the drive, works out what each file is, and copies it into the right place in the structure. Copies — the client drive is not modified.

Feeding it afterwards

Update & Ingest New Files is for the second delivery and the third. It looks at what is already in the project and brings across only what is new, so re-running it on the same drive is safe and quick.

While it runs

A large ingest takes a while. Pause and Resume work, and pausing is safe — a paused ingest is not a half-copied file.

You can leave the tab. The job carries on and the progress is still there when you come back.

Image sequences

A 1,200-frame EXR sequence is one item to Slate, not 1,200 files. That is why the counts look smaller than the file count on the drive, and it is also why ingesting the same sequence twice does not duplicate it.

rename_tool.title: CAP Rename
rename_tool.content:
CAP Rename

Batch renaming, in two modes. Both preview before they touch anything, and the preview is the point — read it before you press the button.

Search and replace

Find a string in the filenames and replace it. The table shows the old name and the new name side by side for every file.

If two files would end up with the same name, Slate says so and refuses rather than overwriting one with the other.

Serialize (make sequence)

Renumber a set of files into a clean, padded sequence — SH_010.1001.exr, SH_010.1002.exr, and so on. Set the base name, the starting frame and the padding.

Sequences

An image sequence is treated as one row. Renaming it renames every frame, and the frame numbers stay in step. You do not select 1,200 files.

Undo

There is no undo button. Renaming happens on disk, and Slate cannot take it back once it is done — which is why the preview exists and why it is worth reading.

stock_browser.title: Stock Viewer
stock_browser.content:
Stock Viewer

The studio's stock library: footage, elements, textures, anything reused across jobs.

Finding something

The search box reaches into the metadata as well as the filename, so searching for 4K or smoke finds clips nobody thought to name that way. Filter by file type to cut a large library down.

Tags

Tags are how the library stays usable at size. Add them as you go; they are shared with the studio, not local to you, so tagging something well saves somebody else the search.

Thumbnails

Generated in the background the first time an item is seen and cached afterwards. A fresh library is slow to look at once and quick every time after.

If a thumbnail never appears, the file is probably a format FFmpeg on this machine cannot read. Everything else about the item still works.

shot_review.title: Timeline Viewer
shot_review.content:
Timeline Viewer

Lay a reel out in order and watch it.

Building a lineup

Pick the project and the reel. Slate finds the current version of each shot and puts them in shot order. It follows what the dashboard says is current, so the lineup reflects the actual state of the reel rather than whatever was last on disk.

Playing it

Heavy EXR and DPX sequences are transcoded to a proxy in the background the first time, then scrub smoothly. The first play of a new shot waits for that; later ones do not.

Cutting

Launch Editor opens the lineup in Olive, embedded in the Slate window. If Olive is not installed, Slate falls back to its own player and the button is absent — ask IT to run setup.bat, which fetches it.

Where OpenRV is available, a shot can be pushed to it for review instead, and a verdict recorded there comes back into Slate against the shot.

dashboard.title: VFX Dashboard
dashboard.content:
VFX Dashboard

Every shot in the project, its status, and who has it.

Reading it

The chips along the top count the reel by status — approved, WIP, review, retake, omit, final, done. They respond to whatever filter is on, so they always describe what you are looking at rather than the whole project.

Each department gets its own column. A cell holds the status for that department on that shot, so you can read one shot across or one department down.

Filtering

Scope, Status and Group narrow the table. Advanced combines them — everything in Matchmove that is WIP and assigned to nobody, for instance. Board View shows the same data as columns by status instead of a table.

Changing something

Edits are held until you press Save Changes, so a mis-click is not immediately everybody's problem. The button is only enabled when there is something to save.

Where the data comes from

The studio database, or an Excel sheet where a show still runs that way. The header says which. In database mode other people's changes arrive without a refresh; in Excel mode the sheet is the truth and Sync reconciles it.

scheduling.title: Scheduling
scheduling.content:
Scheduling

Who is on what, and when.

Assignments here are the same records the dashboard shows against each shot — assigning somebody in one place shows up in the other, because there is only one record.

Approved leave is on the plan

Somebody with approved leave shows as away for those dates. That is the point of the two systems being one application: a plan that does not know about leave is a plan that breaks the week somebody goes on holiday.

Pending leave is not shown as away, because it has not been decided.

bidding.title: Bidding
bidding.content:
Bidding

What a job should cost, before it is agreed.

Build the bid out of shots and the work each one needs by department. Slate totals days and cost as you go.

Afterwards

A bid that turns into a job carries its shot list into the project, so the dashboard starts with the shots that were actually quoted rather than a blank sheet somebody retypes.

Keep the bid after delivery. The difference between what was bid and what the dashboard ended up recording is the only honest input to the next bid.

joining_leaving.title: Joining & Leaving
joining_leaving.content:
Joining & Leaving

One checklist, read in two directions. HR and IT each see their own half, and neither is shown work they cannot do.

Starting somebody

HR only. Start joining puts a person on the list — pick them, say whether they are staff or freelance, and name the department. Freelancers skip payroll and final settlement automatically.

IT do not start people. That division is the point: IT provisioning somebody nobody hired is how ghost accounts happen.

The two halves

HRIT
Signed contract received
ID and address proof
Added to payroll
Studio induction
Introduced to the team		 Domain account created
Email and calendar
Workstation issued
DCC software installed
Project shares mounted
Render farm access

The Yours column counts what is on your list; All counts both, so you can see whether somebody is actually ready to start.

Issuing a machine

IT only. Select the person, press Issue machine, pick from what is free. Slate then records the assignment, marks the machine Active against that person in Hardware, ticks Workstation issued, and stamps the machine name on the row.

That last part is why leaving works. When that person goes, the leaving checklist already knows which machine to ask for — nobody has to remember.

A machine flagged Repair is never offered, and collecting one back does not clear that flag.

When somebody leaves

Start leaving lays down the mirror image. Not a different list — the same one undone. Every access granted on the way in has a revocation on the way out, which is the only reason offboarding can be systematic rather than approximate.

A red Kit not returned card appears at the top when a machine is still out with somebody being offboarded. It is only there when it is true.

hardware.title: Hardware
hardware.content:
Hardware

The studio's machines, and who has them.

Status

StatusMeans
AvailableIn stock, free to issue
ActiveIssued to somebody and in use
RepairWith a workshop. Never offered when issuing, even once it is handed back

Issuing and collecting

Do it from Joining & Leaving rather than here. That way the assignment is recorded against the person and their checklist, and the leaving list knows what to ask for. Editing assigned_to here changes the label without creating the record.

Live status

Machines running the Slate agent report themselves — specification, and whether they are up. A machine that has never reported has been added by hand, which is fine; it just has less detail.

licences.title: Licences
licences.content:
Licences

Not an inventory. This screen answers the two questions you actually get asked, and they cost money in opposite directions:

  • Are we licensed? More people working than seats bought ends in an audit letter.
  • Are we paying for seats nobody uses? Invisible until somebody looks at the peak rather than the total.

Peak, not total

The honest measure of a floating licence is peak concurrent use. Twenty artists and eight Nuke seats is fine if never more than eight are comping at once — and the only way to know is to have written the number down repeatedly.

Record usage does that. Take the reading when the studio is busy; a quiet-afternoon number makes an over-subscribed licence look fine.

The findings

FindingMeans
Over-subscribedMore in use than we own. Outranks everything else — an expiry is a diary entry, a shortfall is people unable to work
ExpiredAlready gone. Anyone relying on it is stuck
Renews soonInside 45 days. Decide before purchasing needs lead time
Under-usedPeak never reaches 60% of what was bought. Seats to drop at renewal
No readingsBought, never measured. Nothing to renew against except the invoice

Every row carries a sentence in numbers, because a status word on its own is not something you can take to purchasing.

deployment.title: Deployment
deployment.content:
Deployment

Getting a new version of Slate onto the studio's machines.

How it works

Clients check a manifest on the studio server at startup. When it names a version newer than the one they are running, they fetch it and apply it on the next restart — nobody walks to a desk.

Rolling one out

  1. Publish the build to the update path.
  2. Update the manifest.
  3. Watch the machines pick it up here.

The table shows which version each machine is actually on, which is the only way to find the workstation somebody switched off for a fortnight.

Do it at the right time

An update applies on restart, so a mid-afternoon rollout reaches artists in the middle of a shot. Publish in the evening.

users_roles.title: Users & Roles
users_roles.content:
Users & Roles

Who exists, and what each of them can reach.

Roles decide screens

A role carries a set of permissions, and permissions decide which tabs are registered at all. This is what makes HR see the leave queue and an artist see their own balance behind the same sidebar entry.

A tab somebody has no business on is absent, not greyed out. A locked entry is an invitation to ask why.

Adding somebody

Create the person here, then start them in Joining & Leaving so the contract, the machine and the accounts are all tracked rather than remembered.

Passwords

Stored as one-way hashes. You can reset somebody's password; you cannot read it, and neither can anyone else.

Somebody who has left

Disable rather than delete. Deleting detaches them from the leave, tickets and assignments that record what happened — and the leaving checklist is what disables the account anyway.

admin_panel.title: Admin Panel
admin_panel.content:
Admin Panel

The studio's own machinery. Everything here affects everybody, so it asks before it acts.

Database

Connection health, the pool, and the audit log. If the client says it is in fallback mode, the reason is visible here.

Circuit breaker open means five database calls failed in a row and Slate stopped trying for a minute rather than making every screen wait. It recovers on its own. If it keeps happening the database is unwell, not Slate.

Backups

Run one, and see when the last one ran. A backup you have never restored is a hope rather than a backup — restore one somewhere safe occasionally.

Logs

Client logs collected centrally, so a problem on somebody's machine can be read without visiting it. This is the first place to look when a ticket says "it crashed" and nothing else.

Templates

The folder structures Build & Ingest offers. Changing one affects every project built afterwards and none built already.

tester.title: Tester Panel
tester.content:
Tester Panel

Tools for checking Slate itself. Nothing here is needed to do a day's work, and some of it writes to the studio database — read the screen before pressing anything.

Data generator

Makes realistic demo projects, shots, tickets and leave so a screen can be looked at before a studio has its own data. Everything it writes is tagged, and it can remove exactly what it wrote.

Workflow simulation

Drives a whole job end to end — ingest, assign, review, deliver — so a change can be checked against the full path rather than one screen.

Diagnostics

Database round trip, disk throughput, thumbnail rate, memory. Useful numbers to put in a ticket when somebody says Slate is slow, because "slow" on its own cannot be acted on.

Chaos

Deliberately breaks things — pulls the database mid-save, corrupts a sequence — to check Slate fails honestly instead of quietly. Never run this against the studio database.

workspace_info.title: Workspace Info
workspace_info.content:
Workspace Info

What this copy of Slate is actually running: the version, where it is installed, which database it reached, and which plugins loaded.

What it is for

Two things.

Answering "which version are you on?" — the first question IT will ask on a ticket, and the one nobody can ever answer. It is on this screen. Copy it into the ticket and save a round trip.

Checking the plugin system. This tab is itself a plugin, shipped as a working example. If it loaded, the plugin machinery is healthy.

Reading it

The card lists the runtime context Slate handed the plugin — the signed-in user, the workspace root, and the active database mode.

Database mode is the one worth glancing at. If it says SQLite when your studio runs PostgreSQL, this machine is on its local fallback copy and nothing it does is being shared. That is worth a ticket.
